newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Chase, Citicorp profits rise in quarter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chase, Citicorp profits rise in quarter.

text.p: Chase Manhattan Corp. and Citicorp, the two largest U.S. banking companies, Tuesday reported strong quarterly earnings, but Wells Fargo & Co. posted disappointing results.

Chase Manhattan, the largest U.S. bank in terms of assets, said it earned $927 million in the first quarter, including restructuring costs related to its merger with Chemical Banking Corp. in March 1996.
This compared with a loss of $89 million in the year-ago quarter, which included a merger-related after-tax charge of $1.03 billion and $70 million in special items.
Operating net income rose 9 percent to $946 million from $867 million in the 1996 first quarter.
Earnings per share rose to $2.02 from $1.82.
"First-quarter earnings reflect the benefits of Chase's balanced business portfolio, with key wholesale and retail areas contributing solid results," said Chairman Walter Shipley.

"While revenue growth in the quarter was lower than our 1997 target, financial performance continues to be strong, as demonstrated by the significant improvement in the efficiency ratio and a higher return on equity."
Total revenue in the first quarter rose to $4.15 billion from $4.04 billion a year ago.

In a sign of possible consumer credit problems ahead, New York-based Chase said its credit card charge-off rate rose to 5.66 percent, compared with 5.11 percent in the fourth quarter and 4.66 percent a year ago.
Expenses fell 2 percent, reflecting merger savings of $205 million and underlying growth of 6 percent, Chase said.

Citicorp, the second-largest banking company, said its net income rose 9 percent to $995 million, or $2.01 a share, in the first quarter despite continued weakness in U.S. consumer credit. This compared with $914 million, or $1.75 a share, in the year-ago period.

"We are accelerating our plans to get fully engaged in our business directions, to offset continuing weakness in the U.S. consumer credit environment plus the need to fund the expansion of our franchise in the emerging markets and the globalization of our processing base," said John Reed, Citicorp's chairman.

Citicorp, also based in New York, said the loss ratio in its U.S. credit card business rose to 5.91 percent in the quarter from 5.45 percent in the 1996 fourth quarter and 4.38 percent in the 1996 first quarter.

Citicorp said its consumer businesses, including its branch banking, credit card business and private bank, earned $490 million in the first quarter, a decline of 3 percent from the 1996 first quarter.
Wells Fargo posted disappointing results as the company's loan and deposit portfolios dropped and some customers left after it acquired First Interstate Bancorp in 1996.
Wells Fargo & Co. said it earned $339 million, or $3.62 a share, for the first quarter, including the effects of the First Interstate merger which was completed on April 1, 1996.
In the year-ago period, the San Francisco-based banking company earned $264 million, or $5.39 a share, but it said the results were not comparable because of the merger.

"We're pleased that we've met our expense reduction target this quarter," said Chairman Paul Hazen. "We are now half-way to our goal of $800 million in gross annual expense reductions. However, due to runoff in our loan and deposit portfolios we are not where we would like to be with respect to revenue."
The disappointing results caused analysts to slash their earnings estimates for Wells Fargo for the year.

"The revenue picture is rather slugglish," said Thomas Theurkauf, an analyst with Keefe Bruyette Woods. "When you strip out securities gains and more volatile items, you find a modest compression in revenues and that's a disappointment."
"It points out how difficult it is for a company to simultaneously strip expenses and grow revenue base (after a merger)," said Theurkauf.

Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank Corp. said its earnings rose to $182 million, or $1.38 a share, in the first quarter, from $169 million, or $1.24 a share, in the year-ago period. The result slightly exceeded Wall Street's consensus estimate of $1.37 a share.
Chase's stock rose $2.125 to $92.625, while Citicorp gained 37.5 cents to $106.875 on the New York Stock Exchange. Wells Fargo fell $6.875 to $257.875, and Mellon rose $2 to $74.75 on the NYSE.
